prompt:
Spring is finally here in Cambridge, and it's time to mow our lawn. For the purpose of these problems, our lawn consists of little clumps of grass arranged in an $m\times n$ rectangular grid, that is, with $m$ rows running east-west and $n$ columns running north-south. To be even more explicit, we might say our clumps are at the lattice points $\{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z^2\mid0\le x<n\text{ and }0\le y<m\}$. Our machinery consists of a fleet of identical mowbots (or \"mobots\" for short). A mobot is a lawn-mowing machine. To mow our lawn, we begin by choosing a *formation*: we place as many mobots as we want at various clumps of grass and orient each mobot's head in a certain direction, either north or east (not south or west). At the blow of a whistle, each mobot starts moving in the direction we've chosen, mowing every clump of grass in its path (including the clump it starts on) until it goes off the lawn. Because the spring is so young, our lawn is rather delicate. Consequently, we want to make sure that every clump of grass is mowed once and only once. We will not consider formations that do not meet this criterion. Two formations are considered \"different\" if there exists a clump of grass for which either (1) for exactly one of the formations does a mobot start on that clump, or (2) there are mobots starting on this clump for both formations, but they are oriented in different directions. As an example, one allowable formation for $m=2$, $n=3$ is the following ($\cdot$ means no mobot starts there; the top row is $y=1$):

$$\begin{array}{ccc}\cdot&\rightarrow&\cdot\\ \uparrow&\rightarrow&\cdot\end{array}$$

Prove that the maximum number of mobots you need to mow your lawn is $m+n-1$.

solutions.title: Last clumps
solutions.body:
Every mobot ends its run on the top row (if it points north) or on the right column (if it points east), and the last clump it mows is its own; different mobots mow different clumps. The top row together with the right column has $m+n-1$ clumps, so there are at most $m+n-1$ mobots.

This is attained: put a north-oriented mobot at each of the $n$ clumps of the top row $y=m-1$ (each mows just its own clump) and an east-oriented mobot at $(0,y)$ for each $y=0,\dots,m-2$ (each mows its whole row). That is $n+m-1$ mobots, and every clump is mowed exactly once. ∎

solutions.title: Diagonal and construction
solutions.body:
*Upper bound:* if $n\le m$, put a north-oriented mobot on each clump of the bottom row $y=0$ ($n$ mobots, each mowing a whole column); if $m\le n$, put an east-oriented mobot on each clump of the left column $x=0$ ($m$ mobots). So $\min\{m,n\}$ mobots suffice.

*Lower bound:* the clumps $(0,0),(1,1),\dots,(k-1,k-1)$ with $k=\min\{m,n\}$ must be mowed by different mobots, because a north-oriented mobot mows clumps with a single $x$-coordinate and an east-oriented mobot clumps with a single $y$-coordinate, while any two of these clumps differ in both coordinates. So at least $k$ mobots are needed. ∎

As an example, one allowable formation for $m=2$, $n=3$ is the following ($\cdot$ means no mobot starts there; the top row is $y=1$):

$$\begin{array}{ccc}\cdot&\rightarrow&\cdot\\ \uparrow&\rightarrow&\cdot\end{array}$$

Prove that, given any formation, each mobot may be colored in one of three colors - say, white, black, and blue - such that no two adjacent clumps of grass are mowed by different mobots of the same color. Two clumps of grass are adjacent if the distance between them is $1$. (In your proof, you may use the Four-Color Theorem if you're familiar with it.)
answer: Greedy coloring along the path of mobots works with $3$ colors.

solutions.title: Greedy coloring
solutions.body:
**Structure of formations.** The clump $(0,0)$ can only be mowed by a mobot starting on it. If that mobot is oriented north it mows column $0$; then no other mobot can start in column $0$ or ever enter it, and the rest is a formation on the lawn formed by columns $1,\dots,n-1$. If it is oriented east it mows row $0$ and the rest is a formation on rows $1,\dots,m-1$. Repeating, the starting points of the mobots form a monotone lattice path $v_0=(0,0),v_1,v_2,\dots$, with $v_{t+1}=v_t+(1,0)$ if the mobot at $v_t$ points north and $v_{t+1}=v_t+(0,1)$ if it points east; the path ends when it leaves the lawn. The mobots are exactly the vertices of this path inside the lawn, and at step $t$ the part of the lawn not yet mowed is the rectangle $[x_t,n-1]\times[y_t,m-1]$ where $v_t=(x_t,y_t)$.

Color the mobots in the order $v_0,v_1,\dots$ of the path. Let $M$ start at $(x,y)$. The clumps of $M$ lie in the unmowed rectangle $[x,n-1]\times[y,m-1]$, so a clump adjacent to a clump of $M$ that was mowed *earlier* lies in column $x-1$ (above row $y$) or in row $y-1$ (right of column $x$). The path left column $x-1$ by a north-oriented mobot $P$ at some $(x-1,y^*)$ with $y^*\le y$, which mows all of column $x-1$ from row $y^*$ up; and it left row $y-1$ by an east-oriented mobot $Q$ at $(x^*,y-1)$ with $x^*\le x$, which mows all of row $y-1$ from column $x^*$ on. So the earlier mobots adjacent to $M$ are among $P$ and $Q$: at most two. Hence when we color $M$, at most two colors are forbidden, and a third color is available. Therefore a valid coloring with $3$ colors exists. ∎

(Alternatively: color the regions of the plane formed by the mowed regions with the Four-Color Theorem; the outside region borders every mobot's region, so at most $3$ colors are used on mobots.)

$$\begin{array}{ccc}\cdot&\rightarrow&\cdot\\ \uparrow&\rightarrow&\cdot\end{array}$$

For $n=m=4$, find a formation with $6$ mobots for which there are exactly $12$ ways to color the mobots in three colors as in problem 3 (i.e. so that no two adjacent clumps are mowed by different mobots of the same color). (No proof is necessary.)

solutions.title: A formation
solutions.body:
Take north-oriented mobots at $(0,0),(1,0),(2,2),(3,2)$ and east-oriented mobots at $(2,0)$ and $(2,1)$. They mow, respectively: column $0$ (call this mobot $A$), column $1$ ($B$), the pair $(2,2),(2,3)$ ($F$), the pair $(3,2),(3,3)$ ($G$), the bottom row from $x=2$ ($C$), and row $1$ from $x=2$ ($D$). Every clump is mowed exactly once.

Two mobots must get different colors iff they are adjacent: $A$-$B$, $B$-$C$, $B$-$D$, $B$-$F$, $C$-$D$, $D$-$F$, $D$-$G$, $F$-$G$. Count colorings: $A$ has $3$ choices, $B$ then $2$. $C$ and $D$ must get the two colors different from $B$ and from each other: $2$ ways. $F$ is adjacent to $B$ and $D$, so it must take the color of $C$ (determined), and $G$ is adjacent to $D$ and $F$ so it takes the color of $B$ (determined). Total $3\cdot2\cdot2=12$.

(Other formations are possible.)

prompt: Suppose we have a regular hexagon and draw all its sides and diagonals. Into how many regions do the segments divide the hexagon? (No proof is necessary.)

solutions.title: Count
solutions.body:
The $6$ short diagonals (joining vertices two apart) form a hexagram whose tips are the hexagon's vertices. Without the long diagonals it cuts the hexagon into: a central regular hexagon, $6$ small triangles at the tips, and $6$ triangles along the sides of the hexagon ($13$ regions). The $3$ long diagonals (through the center) cut the central hexagon into $6$ triangles and cut each of the $6$ tip triangles into $2$ (each long diagonal passes through two opposite tips), and leave the $6$ side triangles untouched. Total: $6+6\cdot2+6=24$.

**Answer: 24**

prompt: Suppose we have an octagon with all angles of $135^\circ$, and consecutive sides of alternating length $1$ and $\sqrt2$. We draw all its sides and diagonals. Into how many regions do the segments divide the octagon? (No proof is necessary.)

solutions.title: Decompose
solutions.body:
View the octagon as five unit squares in a cross arrangement, with four half-squares (isosceles right triangles with legs $1$) wedged at the corners. The diagonals of the octagon cut the central square into $8$ regions, each of the four other squares into $15$ regions, and each of the four half-squares into $4$ regions. The total is $8+4\cdot15+4\cdot4=84$.

**Answer: 84**

prompt: A regular $12$-sided polygon is inscribed in a circle of radius $1$. How many chords of the circle that join two of the vertices of the $12$-gon have lengths whose squares are rational? (No proof is necessary.)

solutions.title: Central angles
solutions.body:
A chord subtending a (minor) central angle $\theta$ has squared length $2-2\cos\theta$ (law of cosines). The possible central angles are $30^\circ,60^\circ,90^\circ,120^\circ,150^\circ,180^\circ$, with $12,12,12,12,12,6$ chords respectively. The squared length is rational for $60^\circ$ ($1$), $90^\circ$ ($2$), $120^\circ$ ($3$), $180^\circ$ ($4$), and irrational for $30^\circ$ and $150^\circ$ ($2\mp\sqrt3$). The count is $12+12+12+6=42$.

**Answer: 42**

prompt: Show a way to construct an equiangular hexagon with side lengths $1,2,3,4,5$, and $6$ (not necessarily in that order).
answer: A $9$-$9$-$9$ equilateral triangle with corners of side $1,2,3$ cut off.

solutions.title: Cut corners off a triangle
solutions.body: An equiangular hexagon is an equilateral triangle with its three corners cut off by lines parallel to the opposite sides (each cut corner is a small equilateral triangle). Start with an equilateral triangle of side $9$ and cut off equilateral triangles of side $1$, $2$ and $3$ from its corners, in this cyclic order around the triangle: the cuts have lengths $1,2,3$, and the remaining pieces of the original sides have lengths $9-1-2=6$, $9-2-3=4$, $9-3-1=5$. The resulting hexagon has all angles $120^\circ$ and sides, in order, $1,6,2,4,3,5$ - which are exactly $1,2,3,4,5,6$. ∎

prompt: Given a convex $n$-gon, $n\ge4$, at most how many diagonals can be drawn such that each drawn diagonal intersects every other drawn diagonal strictly in the interior of the $n$-gon? Prove that your answer is correct.

solutions.title: Construction and bound
solutions.body:
*Construction.* If $n$ is even, draw the $\frac n2$ diagonals joining each vertex to the opposite vertex (they all cross at the center for a regular polygon, and pairwise cross in the interior for any convex polygon). If $n$ is odd, ignore one vertex and do this for the remaining $(n-1)$-gon (its diagonals are still diagonals of the $n$-gon, and they pairwise cross in the interior). This gives $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ diagonals.

*Upper bound.* Two diagonals that meet strictly inside cannot share an endpoint, so the drawn diagonals have pairwise distinct endpoints. A drawn diagonal splits the other $n-2$ vertices into two groups, and every other drawn diagonal must have its endpoints one in each group (to cross it). So on one of the two sides there are at most $\lfloor\frac{n-2}2\rfloor=\lfloor\frac n2\rfloor-1$ vertices, each of which is an endpoint of at most one drawn diagonal, and every other drawn diagonal uses one of them. Hence at most $\lfloor\frac n2\rfloor-1$ other diagonals, plus the first: at most $\lfloor\frac n2\rfloor$ in all. ∎

**Answer: $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$**

prompt: Find the largest positive integer $n$ such that $1!+2!+3!+\cdots+n!$ is a perfect square. Prove that your answer is correct.

solutions.title: Mod 5
solutions.body:
$1!+2!+3!=9=3^2$, so $n=3$ works. For $n\ge4$, every $k!$ with $k\ge5$ is divisible by $5$, so $1!+\cdots+n!\equiv1+2+6+24=33\equiv3\pmod5$. But squares are $0,1,4\pmod5$, so no such sum is a square. Hence the largest $n$ is $3$. ∎

**Answer: 3**

prompt: Find all ordered triples $(x,y,z)$ of positive reals such that $x+y+z=27$ and $x^2+y^2+z^2-xy-yz-zx=0$. Prove that your answer is correct.

solutions.title: Sum of squares
solutions.body:
$x^2+y^2+z^2-xy-yz-zx=\frac12\left[(x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2\right]=0$ forces $x=y=z$, and then $x+y+z=27$ gives $x=y=z=9$. This triple satisfies both equations. ∎

**Answer: (9, 9, 9)**

prompt: Four circles with radii $1$, $2$, $3$, and $r$ are externally tangent to one another. Compute $r$. (No proof is necessary.)

solutions.title: Law of cosines
solutions.body:
Let $A,B,C,P$ be the centers of the circles with radii $1,2,3,r$. Then $AB=3$, $AC=4$, $BC=5$, so $ABC$ is a right triangle with the right angle at $A$, and $PA=1+r$, $PB=2+r$, $PC=3+r$. Since $AB\perp AC$, the direction of $AP$ satisfies $\cos^2\angle PAB+\cos^2\angle PAC=1$, and the law of cosines gives
$$\cos\angle PAB=\frac{3^2+(1+r)^2-(2+r)^2}{2\cdot3(1+r)}=\frac{3-r}{3(1+r)},\qquad\cos\angle PAC=\frac{4^2+(1+r)^2-(3+r)^2}{2\cdot4(1+r)}=\frac{2-r}{2(1+r)}.$$
So $\frac{(3-r)^2}{9(1+r)^2}+\frac{(2-r)^2}{4(1+r)^2}=1$, which simplifies to $23r^2+132r-36=0$, i.e. $(23r-6)(r+6)=0$, so $r=\frac6{23}$.

(Check with Descartes' theorem: $k=\frac11+\frac12+\frac13+2\sqrt{\frac12+\frac16+\frac13}=\frac{11}6+2=\frac{23}6$.)

**Answer: 6/23**

prompt: Find the prime factorization of $$2006^2\cdot2262-669^2\cdot3599+1593^2\cdot1337.$$ (No proof is necessary.)

solutions.title: Factor the polynomial
solutions.body:
Note $2262=669+1593$, $3599=1593+2006$ and $1337=2006-669$. With $a=2006$, $b=669$, $c=-1593$ the expression equals $a^2(b-c)+b^2(c-a)+c^2(a-b)$. This polynomial vanishes when $a=b$, $b=c$ or $c=a$, so it is divisible by $(a-b)(b-c)(a-c)$, and comparing degrees and a test value ($a=2,b=1,c=0$ gives $2$ on both sides) shows it equals $(a-b)(b-c)(a-c)$. Here $a-b=1337$, $b-c=2262$, $a-c=3599$, so the value is $1337\cdot2262\cdot3599$. Now $1337=7\cdot191$, $2262=2\cdot3\cdot13\cdot29$, $3599=60^2-1=59\cdot61$.

**Answer: $2\cdot3\cdot7\cdot13\cdot29\cdot59\cdot61\cdot191$**

prompt: Let $a,b,c,d$ be real numbers so that $c,d$ are not both $0$. Define the function $$m(x)=\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$$ on all real numbers $x$ except possibly $-d/c$, in the event that $c\ne0$. Suppose that the equation $x=m(m(x))$ has at least one solution that is not a solution of $x=m(x)$. Find all possible values of $a+d$. Prove that your answer is correct.

solutions.title: Compare the two equations
solutions.body:
$m(m(x))=\frac{(a^2+bc)x+b(a+d)}{c(a+d)x+bc+d^2}$, so $x=m(m(x))$ becomes $x\left[c(a+d)x+bc+d^2\right]=(a^2+bc)x+b(a+d)$, i.e.
$$(a+d)\left[cx^2+(d-a)x-b\right]=0.$$
The fixed points of $m$ satisfy $x(cx+d)=ax+b$, i.e. $cx^2+(d-a)x-b=0$, the same quadratic. If $a+d\ne0$, every solution of $x=m(m(x))$ would satisfy $cx^2+(d-a)x-b=0$, hence $x=m(x)$ (the excluded point $x=-d/c$ is not a solution of $x=m(m(x))$ anyway). This contradicts the hypothesis. So $a+d=0$.

Conversely $a+d=0$ is possible: $m(x)=-x$ ($a=1$, $d=-1$, $b=c=0$; here $c,d$ are not both $0$) has $m(m(x))=x$ for all $x$, while $x=m(x)$ only for $x=0$. ∎

**Answer: $0$**
